source.title: Layer rotation: a surprisingly simple indicator of generalization in deep networks?

record.file_problem: None; full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a different measured property—layer rotation—tracks generalization across training configurations. It does not test the claim versions’ named interventions or magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results relating layer rotation to generalization; its optimizer, weight-decay and learning-rate comparisons are included where they measure that relationship. Adam moment percentiles and training-speed comparisons do not measure a claim version and are not rows.
record.test_reason: Section 5.4 reports adaptive optimizers’ held-out performance and compares it with SGD plus weight decay, bearing on V4. The central layer-rotation experiments measure a different construct from V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record’s paraphrase is accurate. The authors argue that layer rotation consistently indicates generalization in their experiments, with near-orthogonality to initialization giving the best results, conditional on rotations accompanying training progress. Their feature-learning explanation is preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: Measures layer-level cosine distance from initialization and controls it with Layca; this is not one of the listed original interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer rotation and test performance vary with learning rate, relative layer rotation rates, weight decay, optimizer, and warmup duration; abrupt rotations that do not improve training loss are an exception to the reported relationship.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger layer rotations generally accompany better test accuracy across five image-classification tasks, with exceptions for abrupt rotations that fail to improve training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-level cosine distance from initialization can indicate generalization when rotation accompanies effective training.

fits_no_version.finding: Warmup reduces unstable rotations and improves early training; Layca achieves good generalization without warmup.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controlling layer rotation can stabilize training at high learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: The reduced-MNIST MLP experiment associates larger rotations with better generalization and more prominent learned features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer rotation may indicate the extent of intermediate feature learning.

record.problems: The paper describes most test-accuracy comparisons in prose and figures without exact values or uncertainty estimates. The feature interpretation is based on a preliminary toy experiment. The reported rotation-generalization relationship has an explicit exception for abrupt rotations that do not improve training loss.
record.rows_left_out: Adam second-moment percentile measurements (Figure 5) do not report a generalization outcome. Training-speed comparisons (Figure 7) do not measure the claim versions’ named outcomes. Supplementary LARS results (Figure 12) are not separately rowed because the text reports only a qualitative comparison to Layca, and no claim version names this comparison.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and learned local connectivity.
Language benchmarks, broad optimizer hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, and switching from Adam to SGD. Layca is a separate adaptation.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations of large-batch training.
Controlled dropout comparisons, training-set-size dependence, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap ranking, and comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Removing memorized examples compared with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. Exact task-level test accuracies are not recoverable from the supplied figure text, so the ordinary-optimizer verdict remains aggregate. The comparison with SGD plus weight decay uses the common Layca reference across Figures 3 and 6.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers compared with SGD or momentum SGD under limited tuning, broader tuning, and the stated recovery conditions.
Large-batch versus small-batch outcomes under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and its interaction with training-set size and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: C10-CNN1; C100-resnet; tiny-CNN; C10-CNN2; C100-WRN (five task aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Architectures and depths listed in Table 1; C100-WRN is Wide ResNet 28-10.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with Layca across layer-rotation-rate configurations; compared test accuracy and layer rotation.

conditions.value: ≈ 100% in all configurations, with exceptions reported in Table 2

rows.measure: Test accuracy associated with layer rotation
rows.baseline: Best configuration in each task (α = 0 and ρ(0) = 3−3)
rows.value: Differences of up to 30% test accuracy; larger layer rotations were associated with better generalization, with best performance when nearly all layers reached cosine distance 1.
rows.note: Aggregate result explicitly stated across five tasks; the text does not give the individual test-accuracy values.
rows.check: Layer rotation does not measure any listed version. The near-perfect training-accuracy summary needs its substantial exception: C100-resnet reaches only 82.09% at α = 0.6.

rows.subject: C10-CNN1; C100-resnet; tiny-CNN; C10-CNN2; C100-WRN (five task aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Architectures and depths listed in Table 1; C100-WRN is Wide ResNet 28-10.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with vanilla SGD at different learning rates; compared test accuracy and layer rotation.

conditions.value: Grid search over 10 logarithmically spaced values, except C10-CNN2 and C100-WRN

rows.measure: Test accuracy associated with layer rotation
rows.value: Test accuracy increased with larger layer rotations until a tipping point, then decreased; SGD test performance remained significantly below the Layca optimal configuration despite learning-rate tuning.
rows.note: Authors qualify the rotation relationship: abrupt rotations that do not improve training loss do not follow the rule of thumb.
rows.check: Learning-rate effects on layer rotation and test accuracy do not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: C10-CNN1; C100-resnet; tiny-CNN; C10-CNN2; C100-WRN (five task aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Architectures and depths listed in Table 1; C100-WRN is Wide ResNet 28-10.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD plus weight decay; compared test accuracy and layer rotation.
rows.value: All layers reached cosine distance 1 from initialization; test performances were on par with Layca’s optimal configuration.
rows.note: The paper describes weight decay as enabling large layer rotations during SGD training.
rows.check: This is a useful SGD comparator for R5, but weight decay’s effect on rotation alone does not test a listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet-110
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD using a high learning rate and varying warmup duration; compared layer rotations, training curves and final test accuracy.
rows.measure: Test accuracy alongside layer rotation and training accuracy
rows.value: Without warmup, unstable rotations coincided with no training-accuracy improvement before epoch 25; warmups brought significant improvements, with 75% training accuracy after 25 epochs. Layca reached high generalization performance without warmup.
rows.note: No exact final test-accuracy values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Warmup is varied without a batch-size comparison, so this does not test V5. Separate the training-accuracy outcomes from final test accuracy; the supplied text gives no numerical final test accuracies.

rows.subject: C10-CNN1; C100-resnet; tiny-CNN; C10-CNN2; C100-WRN (five task aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Architectures and depths listed in Table 1; C100-WRN is Wide ResNet 28-10.
rows.operation_detail: Trained with adaptive gradient methods, with and without Layca control; compared test accuracy and layer rotation.

conditions.value: RMSProp, Adam, Adagrad, RMSProp+L2 and Adam+L2, respectively for each task/column

rows.measure: Test accuracy associated with layer rotation
rows.baseline: Layca optimal configuration; SGD + weight decay for adaptive methods with Layca
rows.value: Adaptive methods without Layca showed overall worse generalization than Layca’s optimal configuration, with small and/or non-uniform rotations. With Layca control, adaptive methods reached test accuracies on par with SGD + weight decay.
rows.note: Results are aggregated over five tasks in the prose; no individual test-accuracy values are stated.
rows.check: Incorrectly excluded from V4. Split ordinary adaptive optimization from adaptive optimization with Layca, and separate tasks and optimizers. Ordinary adaptive methods have overall worse generalization than optimal Layca, which R3 reports as comparable to SGD plus weight decay; adding Layca restores comparable performance. The aggregate combines these different outcomes and does not establish a deficit on every task.

rows.subject: 1 hidden layer MLP (784 neurons)
rows.operation_detail: Trained from an identical initialization at four learning rates using Layca; compared learned intermediate features and generalization.
rows.measure: Test generalization associated with layer rotation; qualitative feature visualization
rows.baseline: Four configurations share an identical initialization
rows.value: The configurations had different generalization abilities; the authors report that larger rotations were associated with better generalization. They say rotation appeared to affect the extent to which features were learned, rather than which features were learned.
rows.note: The text gives no exact test-accuracy values for the four configurations.
rows.check: Feature visualization and rotation-associated generalization at fixed width do not test any listed version.

relationships.condition: Ordinary adaptive optimizers across the five image-classification tasks, considered collectively, with learning-rate tuning or prescribed benchmark settings.
relationships.reason: R5 reports overall worse generalization than optimal Layca; R3 supplies the comparable SGD-plus-weight-decay reference. This supports the aggregate tendency, without establishing that every task exhibits it.
relationships.display_finding: In the unverified comparison, adaptive methods reportedly performed worse overall than the best Layca result, while SGD with weight decay was comparable to Layca. The overall results do not establish how the methods ranked on each task.

relationships.condition: Adaptive optimizers with layer rotations controlled by Layca.
relationships.reason: R5 reports test accuracy comparable to SGD plus weight decay after adding Layca, showing that the adaptive-method deficit depends on the training procedure.
relationships.display_finding: Reported test accuracy comparable to SGD with weight decay after adding Layca remains unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
